name: blind-01

seed.title: Mapping AAV capsid-receptor interactions to explain barrier transcytosis versus intracellular retention
seed.text: Basically molecularly mapping the interaction between an agent (the ones we use in the lab) and surface receptors, to understand why certain variants can pass through a cell to the other side while others remain inside the cell. It is complex and requires a dataset that I'm not sure how to obtain. The gap is a matched dataset linking capsid-receptor binding signatures to transcytosis versus intracellular retention in brain microvascular endothelial cells.
seed.root_question: Can molecular mapping of AAV capsid-receptor interactions on brain microvascular endothelial cells determine which AAV variants transcytose across the blood-brain barrier versus remain intracellular, and for which capsid-receptor binding signatures?

chosen.id: Option 1: Exhaustive capsid–receptor complex enumeration (docking and AlphaFold-Multimer)
chosen.title: Exhaustive capsid–receptor complex enumeration (docking and AlphaFold-Multimer)
chosen.text: Enumerate binding modes of engineered capsid libraries against the BBB receptor panel (LY6A, LY6C1, ALPL, LRP6, CA4, AAVR) with docking, MD refinement, and AlphaFold-Multimer to test whether transcytosis-competent pairs share a geometric motif such as 3-fold-axis engagement of GPI-anchored receptors (https://www.voyagertherapeutics.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/05/POSTER-Voyager_ASGCT_2024_FINAL_Ishan.pdf). Published modeling covers only single-digit complexes, e.g. AlphaFold-Multimer models of LRP6 with AAV-X1 and CAP-Mac VR-VIII peptides (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11381518), against an experimental catalog of ~150 AAV capsid structures (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12682079). Narrowing: This leaves aside everything after binding — endosomal sorting, lysosomal degradation, nuclear import — so the computed interface geometry stands in for the binding step alone, not for fate. Its answer still moves the root question because it either widens or closes the catalog of candidate signatures (Q3) against which the sufficiency claim (Q1) must be tested.
chosen.root_link: Bears on Q3 of the root question — for which capsid–receptor binding signatures transcytosis occurs — specifically whether a shared interface motif marks transcytosis-competent complexes.
chosen.compute_open: More parallel compute would buy model runs (capsid × receptor × pose); published measurements of its effect stop at single-digit numbers of AAV–receptor complexes modeled per study — two LRP6 peptide complexes in https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11381518 — and above that it is unknown whether exhaustive enumeration would surface a shared transcytosis-competent motif or demonstrate that no such motif exists.
chosen.sequential: none: every capsid–receptor pair is an independent docking or AlphaFold-Multimer job with its own random seeds, so the work already splits into independent pieces.
chosen.narrowing: This leaves aside everything after binding — endosomal sorting, lysosomal degradation, nuclear import — so the computed interface geometry stands in for the binding step alone, not for fate. Its answer still moves the root question because it either widens or closes the catalog of candidate signatures (Q3) against which the sufficiency claim (Q1) must be tested.

screen.id: Option 2: Microsecond molecular dynamics of capsid–receptor–membrane assemblies
screen.title: Microsecond molecular dynamics of capsid–receptor–membrane assemblies
screen.root_link: Bears on Q1/Q3 — whether fate-relevant physics such as pH-dependent release and membrane-domain partitioning is already visible at the binding step, and so whether molecular mapping can be pushed toward a trafficking signature.
screen.compute_open: settled: longer trajectories are already known to reveal more of the binding configurational space — the AAV2–AAVR coarse-grained study reports that once the capsid is membrane-bound its motion is restricted and much longer simulation times would be required to observe how the capsid moves on the membrane (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11492248).
screen.sequential: One answer waits on a chain of ~2 fs integration steps (the timestep used in the AAV2–AAVR protocol, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11492248), each step consuming the previous step's forces and coordinates, so one 100 ns run is ~5×10^7 sequential steps and a 1 µs run ~5×10^8; the answer needs several independent replicas and a single replica keeps one GPU essentially fully busy (GPU offloading in gmx mdrun, https://manual.gromacs.org/documentation/current/user-guide/mdrun-performance.html). The steps must run in order inside one trajectory, but replicas can run at once and recasting the answer as an ensemble of many short trajectories combined by Markov-state analysis would let them run simultaneously — a payoff only if the dynamics is metastable so short runs recombine — as tried for virus capsid assembly with many short unbiased trajectories run in parallel (https://arxiv.org/pdf/1402.1784).
screen.narrowing: This leaves aside the cell's sorting machinery — retromer/SNX tubule engagement, lysosomal routing — and treats simulated binding/unbinding and membrane partitioning as a stand-in for the trafficking decision. Its answer still moves the root question by testing whether any fate-relevant physics is recoverable from the binding step at all, which is exactly the sufficiency issue Q1 raises.
reasons: compute effect settled: no open compute quantity

screen.title: Supervised sequence-to-transcytosis phenotype models
screen.root_link: Bears on Q2 — assigning each variant a fate — and on whether the binding-to-fate gap in Q1 can be closed statistically instead of mechanistically.
screen.compute_open: More parallel compute would buy model runs (seeds, architectures) and model size; published measurements of its effect stop at ensembles of three architectures over ~2×10^5 labeled variants (https://www.nature.com/articles/s41587-020-00793-4) and six Fit4Function models over ≤240K-variant libraries (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11297966), and above that it is unknown whether more parameters, seeds, or training compute improve transcytosis prediction or whether labeled transcytosis data, not FLOPs, is the binding constraint.
screen.sequential: One training run is a chain of roughly 10^4–10^5 gradient updates, each update waiting on the previous weights' loss, so a converged answer needs multiple independent seeds and one model per trait (Fit4Function trained six, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11297966), and a single run keeps one GPU busy throughout. Within a run the updates must run in order, but different seeds and per-trait models can train at the same time — which pays off when each model fits one GPU and the labeled set is fully visible to every run, the arrangement used by Fit4Function's RNN/LSTM sequence models (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11297966).
screen.narrowing: This leaves aside the mechanism of the sorting decision and treats a predicted transcytosis score as a stand-in for measured transwell/in vivo fate. Its answer still moves the root question because a predictor that generalizes would show which feature set carries fate information, i.e. how far Q3's signatures can be pushed toward Q1's sufficiency claim.

screen.id: Option 4: Cryo-EM reconstruction of capsid–receptor complexes
screen.title: Cryo-EM reconstruction of capsid–receptor complexes
screen.root_link: Bears on the interface-mapping component of Q1 — which capsid residues and receptor domains contact — that feeds the binding signatures of Q3.
screen.compute_open: settled: map resolution is already known to improve as more particles contribute — in the AAV structural atlas, genome-containing AAV7/11/12/13 reconstructions reached slightly lower resolution than the empty capsids specifically because fewer capsids were used in those reconstructions (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7828300).
screen.sequential: One map waits on a chain of processing stages — motion correction, CTF estimation, particle picking, 2D classification, 3D refinement — roughly a dozen sequential stages each consuming the previous stage's particle stack; the answer needs one reconstruction per complex plus re-runs for empty/full or symmetry-broken states (the AAV2 Rep–capsid work produced separate pentameric and hexameric maps, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12713660), and a single refinement keeps one GPU busy for hours to days. The stages must run in order, but per-particle work inside a stage can run simultaneously — as in local refinements of 45,150 and 75,559 symmetry-expanded particles on GPU computing resources (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12713660) — which pays off when a dataset holds tens of thousands of independent particles.
screen.narrowing: This leaves aside affinity, kinetics, and post-binding sorting, so the static interface stands in for the whole binding event. Its answer still moves the root question because residue-level contact maps are the raw material from which any binding signature (Q3) is defined.
reasons: compute effect settled: no open compute quantity

screen.title: Cross-species receptor–capsid compatibility scoring
screen.root_link: Bears on the species-conditionality caveat of Q3 — whether a binding signature learned in mouse survives in human.
screen.compute_open: More parallel compute would buy model runs (receptor-ortholog × capsid pairs scored); published measurements of its effect stop at a handful of isoforms — ALPL contact residues compared for one capsid across human, cynomolgus macaque, and mouse (https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2024.03.12.584703v1.full.pdf) — and above that it is unknown whether exhaustive ortholog scoring would keep, drop, or reorder the GPI-anchored-protein and LRP6 signatures as candidates for human BBB crossing.
screen.sequential: none: each receptor-ortholog × capsid pair is an independent alignment and modeling job, so the work already splits into independent pieces.
screen.narrowing: This leaves aside mouse-only biology such as Ly6a polymorphism underlying strain-specific PHP.B tropism (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31696742) and treats interface conservation as a stand-in for actual human transcytosis. Its answer still moves the root question because translatability is a necessary filter on any signature Q3 proposes for human use.

screen.title: Full-capsid, membrane-anchored receptor enumeration of the 3-fold GPI engagement motif
screen.changes: Changes the system studied — full 60-mer capsid with a GPI-anchored receptor in a membrane patch at the 3-fold spike, instead of isolated AA587–594 peptides. This closes the named gap that a 'shared 3-fold motif' may partly reflect the peptide-competition setup, and it matters to the Gradinaru/APPRAISE programme, whose current pipeline is peptide-based, and to Voyager's capsid–receptor mechanism step, which reads real capsid engagement.
screen.root_link: Bears on Q3 of the root question — which capsid–receptor binding signatures permit transcytosis — by asking whether the shared 3-fold-axis GPI-engagement motif is a property of the intact capsid engaging a membrane receptor rather than of peptide competition.
screen.compute_open: More parallel compute buys full-capsid × receptor × pose jobs, which are far more expensive per model than peptide jobs; published measurements of depth effects stop at single-digit peptide complexes per study, and above that it is unknown whether whole-capsid sampling preserves, sharpens or dissolves the shared-motif call.
screen.sequential: none: every full-capsid–receptor pose is an independent docking or AlphaFold-Multimer job with its own random seeds.
screen.narrowing: Leaves aside everything after binding — endosomal sorting, lysosomal degradation, nuclear import — so the computed interface geometry stands in only for the binding step. It still moves the root question because it decides whether the candidate signature catalog (Q3) survives when the capsid is modeled as it actually engages the receptor, which sets what Q1's sufficiency claim has to test.

screen.title: Motif call judged against matched human Transwell transcytosis labels on conserved ALPL
screen.changes: Changes the comparison it is judged against — matched human Transwell transcytosis measurements built around Voyager's VCAP-102±ALPL versus AAV9 result, instead of scarce mixed-species phenotype labels. This closes the label-scarcity gap and the species gap (ALPL is conserved while LY6A/LY6C1 are mouse-restricted and 9P31/9P36 bind mouse but not primate CA4), and it targets Voyager's TRACER / ALPL NeuroShuttle mechanism-of-action step and Dyno's ALPL mechanism assignment.
screen.root_link: Bears on Q1 and Q3 of the root question — whether a binding signature is sufficient for transcytosis — by asking whether the 3-fold-axis GPI-engagement gap separates transcytosis-competent from retained pairs when labels come from human endothelium and a conserved receptor.
screen.compute_open: More parallel compute buys pose models across the expanded, label-matched ALPL pair set (72 pairs at 144, 720 and 2,880 models); previously only a single transcytosis pair existed to compare against, so whether a motif emerges once labels are measured in the same human assay is unknown.
screen.sequential: none: each capsid–receptor pose is an independent docking or AlphaFold-Multimer job, and the Transwell measurements are a separate bench block that does not gate the pose sweep.
screen.narrowing: Leaves aside post-binding fate beyond the barrier readout and any receptor without a matched transcytosis measurement, so the observable stands in for transcytosis rate across human endothelium rather than for in vivo brain transduction. It moves the root question because it converts Q1's sufficiency claim into a test on human-relevant pairs instead of mouse-restricted signatures.

screen.title: Motif calls emitted for Capsida NR001–NR005 and Lir Starfish binding-assay readouts
screen.changes: Changes the programme it is aimed at — output is scored against Capsida's NR001–NR005 human BBB-receptor platform and Lir's Starfish docking pipeline instead of against phenotype labels. This closes the named gap that these two additional consumers were not assessed and that binding-only, human-relevant receptors are exactly what their assays read.
screen.root_link: Bears on Q3 of the root question — which capsid–receptor binding signatures are candidates for transcytosis — by pruning the catalog to pairs that survive a real human-receptor binding assay before any transcytosis claim (Q1) is attempted.
screen.compute_open: More parallel compute buys model runs across capsid × receptor × pose for the NR001–NR005 receptor set, letting the shared-motif question be tested receptor by receptor against binding readouts rather than at a single receptor; published depth effects stop at single-digit complexes and the proprietary pipelines are unmeasured, so the payoff is unknown.
screen.sequential: none: each capsid–receptor pose is an independent docking or AlphaFold-Multimer job with its own seeds, and the plate/bead binding readouts are a separate block.
screen.narrowing: Leaves aside transcytosis and all post-binding fate — the observable is binding agreement plus interface geometry, not fate. It still moves the root question by narrowing the candidate signature catalog (Q3) to pairs that survive a human-receptor binding assay, which is the precondition for any sufficiency test (Q1).

frame_best.name: Gradinaru Lab (Caltech) / APPRAISE-AAV — receptor-directed AAV engineering and the open-source APPRAISE package
frame_best.step: The computational step the card scales: ranking engineered capsid insertion peptides against BBB receptors by AlphaFold-Multimer pairwise competition modeling, scored with atom-counting energy plus binding-angle and pocket-depth geometry, used to classify receptor-dependent vs receptor-independent capsids and to pick candidates before in vivo selection. Today this runs at ten models per competition on single-GPU Colab sessions; the card asks whether 144–2,880 pose models per pair change the transcytosis call.

frame_programmes.name: Voyager Therapeutics — TRACER capsid discovery and ALPL NeuroShuttle (VCAP-102 / VY1706)
frame_programmes.step: Mechanism-of-action step of the TRACER pipeline the card targets: after RNA-guided in vivo capsid evolution, Voyager identifies the vascular receptor each capsid uses to cross the BBB and demonstrates that binding of that receptor initiates transcytosis rather than mere uptake — i.e., the transcytose-versus-retain call per capsid–receptor pair. In practice this is done with human surface-protein binding/transduction screens, SPR, and a polarized cell-barrier Transwell assay, not with exhaustive structural enumeration.

frame_programmes.name: Gradinaru Lab (Caltech) / APPRAISE-AAV — receptor-directed AAV engineering and the open-source APPRAISE package
frame_programmes.step: The computational step the card scales: ranking engineered capsid insertion peptides against BBB receptors by AlphaFold-Multimer pairwise competition modeling, scored with atom-counting energy plus binding-angle and pocket-depth geometry, used to classify receptor-dependent vs receptor-independent capsids and to pick candidates before in vivo selection. Today this runs at ten models per competition on single-GPU Colab sessions; the card asks whether 144–2,880 pose models per pair change the transcytosis call.

frame_programmes.name: Dyno Therapeutics — multi-mechanism BBB-crossing capsid portfolio (ALPL, TfR1, Dyno-discovered receptors)
frame_programmes.step: The step the card targets is Dyno's mechanism assignment and structure-aware design for its CNS portfolio: deciding which BBB receptor each engineered capsid engages and whether that engagement crosses the BBB, then engineering capsids for several BBB-crossing mechanisms in parallel (ALPL, hTfR1, and Dyno-discovered receptors) rather than one pathway. Dyno states it integrates sequence- and structure-based approaches in its generative design, with receptor mechanism confirmed by head-to-head in vivo comparisons.

gaps: No published pose-depth (model-count) scaling study for AAV capsid–receptor complexes exists; the closest comparators are 10 AF-Multimer models per competition (Ding et al. 2024) and 5 models with up to 20 recycles for LRP6 complexes (Shay et al. 2024), so the card's 144–2,880 arms have no prior baseline beyond the ten-model published one.

Per-pair transcytose-versus-retain phenotype labels are scarce: Voyager's MDCK Transwell result covers VCAP-102±ALPL vs AAV9 only, and most programs (Dyno, Capsida, Gradinaru) score in vivo brain transduction rather than transcytosis rate, so the card's training labels may rest on few direct measurements.

APPRAISE-style modeling uses isolated VR-VIII peptides (AA587–594), not the full 60-mer capsid at the 3-fold spike with GPI anchor and membrane; a 'shared 3-fold motif' may partly reflect the peptide-competition setup, and weak avidity-dependent contacts can evade prediction (the card's own caveat).

Species gaps limit motif generality: LY6A/LY6C1 are mouse-restricted (absent in primates), 9P31/9P36 bind mouse but not primate CA4, while ALPL is conserved — a motif validated on mouse GPI receptors may not transfer to human-relevant pairs.

Dyno's and Capsida's structural pipelines are proprietary, so 'already done' cannot be settled for them; Capsida's NR001–NR005 human BBB-receptor platform with plate-/bead-based capsid/receptor binding assays (capsida.com) and Lir's Starfish capsid-structure/docking pipeline (lirtx.com) are additional consumers of this result that were not assessed in depth here.

frame_best.name: Lir Therapeutics — Starfish™ / nAAVigator®
frame_best.step: Starfish™ capsid-surface structure generation feeding receptor docking on symmetry-axis patches inside the nAAVigator® pipeline — in Lir's words, surface portions 'at the 2, 3 and 5-fold axes are the minimum subunit for useful docking or structural assessment of capsid stability in silico'. Docking receptors onto those Starfish-built variant capsid surfaces produces the binding-screen hits and 'explainability' that drive Lir's lab-in-the-loop variant selection. The card scores exactly this docking/binding-call step and its threefold-axis interface geometry.

frame_programmes.name: Capsida Biotherapeutics
frame_programmes.step: In vitro capsid–receptor binding detection in their integrated platform: plate-based and bead-based receptor binding assays ('In Vitro Binding Platform Demonstrates Reproducible Capsid/Receptor Binding Data Consistent with Expression Profiles') that emit bind/no-bind readouts for engineered capsids against the NR001–NR005 blood-brain-barrier receptor panel, with in vitro binding predictive power confirmed by transduction in receptor-expressing cell lines. The card emits computed capsid–receptor binding calls in exactly this readout's format, so its result would sit directly upstream of this step as an in silico pre-filter.

frame_programmes.name: Lir Therapeutics — Starfish™ / nAAVigator®
frame_programmes.step: Starfish™ capsid-surface structure generation feeding receptor docking on symmetry-axis patches inside the nAAVigator® pipeline — in Lir's words, surface portions 'at the 2, 3 and 5-fold axes are the minimum subunit for useful docking or structural assessment of capsid stability in silico'. Docking receptors onto those Starfish-built variant capsid surfaces produces the binding-screen hits and 'explainability' that drive Lir's lab-in-the-loop variant selection. The card scores exactly this docking/binding-call step and its threefold-axis interface geometry.

frame_programmes.name: CLOVER Center / Gradinaru Laboratory, Caltech — APPRAISE
frame_programmes.step: Computed capsid–receptor binding models and bind/no-bind calls: the APPRAISE pipeline ranks engineered capsid peptides by receptor-binding propensity from AlphaFold-Multimer competitions ('a method that predicts the receptor binding propensity of engineered proteins based on high-precision protein structure prediction tools, such as AlphaFold2-multimer'), extended to integrative trimer–receptor models on the AAV threefold spike, and validated against cell-microarray/SPR/pull-down labels and cryo-ET binding sites. This is the programme the card's closest prior (Shay et al. 2024) belongs to, and its computed-call step is the one the card scales from a handful of models to 54–432 runs.

gaps: Public bind/no-bind labels cover only 13 of the card's 36 pairs, and Capsida's NR001–NR005 receptor identities are patented and unnamed publicly, so the full grid can never be scored against Capsida's own plate/bead labels.
None of the three programmes has published a run-count scaling curve (54→432 model runs) for binding-call accuracy, so the card's lever question is open for all of them.

Lir's Starfish benchmarks and receptor-docking screens live in blog posts and an ESGCT 2025 poster, not a peer-reviewed bind/no-bind accuracy dataset, so its call accuracy is not externally checkable before the card's test.
The card yields binding-call agreement and interface geometry only; all three programmes ultimately gate on transduction, transcytosis or in vivo data that the card does not supply.

Capsida's current priority receptors (ADAM15 for CAP-002, RECK for its next-generation capsid) are absent from the card's reference labels and from public interface structures, so even a positive lever result would not validate calls for the pairs Capsida is now prioritizing.
